source.title: Moving the Safety Barrier: Dynamic Routing Adaptive Alignment Against White-Box Attacks
source.authors: Shang-Ze Li; Chuan-Cheng Shi; Si-Miao Xie; Ling-Zhi He; Chengxin Ji; Zi-Feng Cheng; Fei Shen; Chao Wu; T. Chua

record.tranche_reason: The paper applies ABLATE, described as removing a single refusal direction from the residual stream across all layers and token positions, and reports harmful-response outcomes on additional models.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are the ABLATE attack outcomes in Table V. The paper does not report results for adding a direction, and DRAA's general-capability results do not measure capability after this direction is ablated. Other attack outcomes and DRAA training results do not test the specific direction intervention.
record.test_reason: The paper applies ABLATE, citing Arditi et al. [2]: one refusal direction is removed from the residual stream at all layers and token positions. It reports harmful-response counts on StrongREJECT (313 prompts, LLaMA-Guard-3 judge) for Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.2-3B. Their own unablated ORI counts (Tables I/II) serve as the baseline, so the results bear on whether direction ablation removes refusal in these models. This is the same intervention with a close harmful-response measure. The study is a defense paper, but it reports the Original models' results, not only its own method.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors present ABLATE as one of three unseen white-box attacks and say DRAA achieves the lowest success under all of them. On Qwen2.5-7B, DRAA's margin under ABLATE is only 4 cases (291 vs 295); the text does not flag this.
record.recipe_differences: The paper describes the ABLATE intervention as removing one refusal direction from the residual stream across all layers and positions, but does not state how that direction is computed or provide a direction-specific unablated comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ABLATE outcomes differ across model families and model variants.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety fine-tuning that targets MLP neuron routes (RLHF-Safety, SafeNeuron, DRAA) cuts direction-ablation success on LLaMA-3.2-3B (133 to 37–113) but barely on Qwen2.5-7B (299 to 291–296).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness to refusal-direction ablation from neuron-level safety training is model-dependent; on some models it does not transfer.

record.problems: The ABLATE results are reported as attack-success counts without an unablated comparison for the same models in Table V or uncertainty estimates. General capability is reported for DRAA under other evaluations, not after ABLATE.
record.rows_left_out: GRAD and WANDA results in Table V were left out because those attacks are not described as suppressing the single refusal direction. Other safety and capability tables concern DRAA or other neuron-pruning settings, not the single-direction intervention.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; capability after ablation; how the direction was extracted (difference-in-means is assumed via the citation, not stated).
Whether jailbreaks suppress the direction, and whether training against its ablation adds robustness. Neither is tested: DRAA trains against neuron-route masking.

missing.what: Unablated (ORI) harmful-response counts for the same Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.2-3B variants. These are needed as baselines for the ABLATE rows.
missing.locator: Table I (Qwen2.5-7B ORI column) and Table II (LLaMA-3.2-3B ORI column)

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The direction-extraction method is not described; it is only cited to [2] and called a rank-one intervention. No uncertainty is reported. Harmful responses were judged by LLaMA-Guard-3-8B with human review.

versions.untested_parts: The reported intervention tests removal, not addition; the text does not state how the refusal direction was identified or test whether it is a difference-in-means direction. General capability after ablating that direction is not reported.

The paper reports an attack that removes a single refusal direction, but does not test whether other attacks suppress that direction or whether training against this direction's ablation adds robustness.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Qwen2.5-7B, original and all safety-trained variants
labels.reason: ORI 0–16/313 rises to 291–299/313 under ABLATE (Table I vs Table V), which is near-complete removal. Induction and capability retention are not tested, so they are untested rather than limits_scope.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.reason: ORI 1–7/313 rises only to 37–133/313 (Original 6 -> 133), a clear but incomplete effect, so this is not challenges. The direction recipe is not stated, so the weakness may come from the recipe.

relation.reason: ABLATE is used as an attack against the authors' defense, but the study also reports harmful-response counts for the unmodified Original models. Together with the ORI counts in Tables I/II, these bear directly on whether ablation removes refusal.

tranche.reason: ABLATE is cited to Arditi et al. [2]: one refusal direction projected out of the residual stream at all layers and token positions. It is scored as Llama-Guard-judged harmful responses, which matches the original's safety score. How the direction is extracted is not stated, beyond 'activation-guided' and being re-localized on each evaluated model, so the recipe is close rather than exact.

source_check.notes: The unablated baselines come from the ORI columns of Tables I/II. Table V gives only post-attack counts, judged by LLaMA-Guard-3-8B plus human review on 313 StrongREJECT prompts, with no uncertainty and no capability results under ABLATE. On LLaMA-3.2-3B, GRAD/WANDA reach 303–305/313 for the non-DRAA models while ABLATE reaches only 55–133, which points to a weak ABLATE recipe on this model. The authors_conclusion says the 4-case Qwen margin goes unflagged; the text does state it ('by 39, 6, and 4 cases') but does not comment on its size.

statements.correction: LLaMA-3.2-3B Original 6/313 -> 133/313; SN-Tune 7 -> 88, RLHF-Safety 2 -> 55, SafeNeuron 1 -> 113, DRAA 1 -> 37 (Table II ORI vs Table V ABLATE). Cite TV-Llama-SafeNeuron and TV-Llama-DRAA as well.
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right. But the 37–113/313 range comes from TV-Llama-DRAA (37) and TV-Llama-SafeNeuron (113), and neither is in the cited rows.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: ABLATE yields 295–299 successful attacks out of 313 for the listed Qwen2.5-7B variants, consistent with substantial refusal disruption (TV-Qwen-Orig, TV-Qwen-SNTune, TV-Qwen-RLHF, TV-Qwen-SafeNeuron, TV-Qwen-DRAA).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The reported outcomes are lower and vary across variants, from 37/313 to 133/313 successful attacks, so the intervention does not show near-complete refusal disruption consistently across these models (TV-Llama-Orig, TV-Llama-SNTune, TV-Llama-RLHF, TV-Llama-SafeNeuron, TV-Llama-DRAA).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qwen2.5-7B models under the ABLATE attack
reader_labels.reason: The direction-removal attack reports 291–299 successful attacks out of 313 on the Qwen2.5-7B variants (TV-Qwen-Orig, TV-Qwen-SNTune, TV-Qwen-RLHF, TV-Qwen-SafeNeuron, TV-Qwen-DRAA).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LLaMA-3.2-3B models under the ABLATE attack
reader_labels.reason: Successful attacks range from 37/313 to 133/313 across the listed LLaMA-3.2-3B variants, indicating that the direction-removal attack's outcome is model-dependent (TV-Llama-Orig, TV-Llama-SNTune, TV-Llama-RLHF, TV-Llama-SafeNeuron, TV-Llama-DRAA).
